name: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
venue: arXiv 2305.16291 (May 2023); later published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2024
authors_affiliation: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi 'Jim' Fan, Anima Anandkumar. Primary affiliations: NVIDIA; with Caltech, UT Austin, Stanford, and UW Madison.
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager (single-branch research repo, last meaningful commits 2023; not a continuously-updated leaderboard/paper-list)
task_domain: Embodied agent / open-ended lifelong learning and embodied control in Minecraft (high-level code-as-action planning via the Mineflayer API).
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent, open-ended lifelong learning in the Minecraft sandbox without human intervention and without model fine-tuning. The agent (GPT-4 via blackbox queries) continuously explores, proposes its own tasks via an automatic curriculum, writes executable JavaScript skills, and reuses them. No task-success supervision is given: success is judged by a self-verification LLM critic. Setting is online/test-time: the skill library starts empty and grows during deployment. A separately learned (accumulated) skill library can also be loaded into a fresh world for zero-shot task solving.
what_is_retrieved: Reusable skills, each represented as a self-contained executable JavaScript/code function (temporally-extended, compositional behavior) plus an LLM-generated natural-language description used as the retrieval key.
retrieval_grounding: GROWING / episodic-procedural memory written by the agent itself (an ever-growing skill library). It is not a static external corpus; the agent adds verified skills online. (Control-primitive APIs are a fixed set always available in the prompt, but the retrieved skills come from the growing library.)
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-k ranking: a constant top-5 similarity retrieval (retrieval_top_k=5). No completeness/minimal-set objective and no precision-driven variable-size selection; k is a fixed hyperparameter (capped at the current library size when fewer than 5 skills exist).
retrieval_unit: skill-or-program: a complete executable code skill (an async JavaScript function that scaffolds a temporally-extended behavior for a curriculum-proposed task), indexed by the embedding of its NL description.
index_source: Growing memory induced online/at test-time: the skill vector store starts empty and is populated as GPT-4 generates and self-verifies new skills during lifelong learning. Not offline-induced; not a static corpus.
index_structure_topology: Flat vector index. Skills are stored in a Chroma vector database (collection 'skill_vectordb'); each entry's key is the embedding of the program description and the value is the program code stored on disk / in skills.json. No graph, hierarchy, or clustering over skills.
retriever_type: Dense embedding retriever: OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings with cosine/L2 similarity search over a Chroma vector store (similarity_search_with_score). Off-the-shelf, not learned.
retriever_learning_signal: None (off-the-shelf). The embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002) is frozen and not trained or fine-tuned; retrieval is fixed top-k similarity with no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signal.
query_construction: Query is a synthetic, expanded context: GPT-3.5 first generates a general suggestion / task plan for solving the new task proposed by the automatic curriculum, which is combined with environment feedback; the embedding of this self-generated plan + environment feedback is used as the retrieval query. (The skill key is itself a GPT-3.5-generated program description embedding.)
query_granularity: Task-level: one retrieval per newly proposed task (the automatic-curriculum objective), conditioned on a generated plan and current environment feedback; not per-step or per-token.
when_to_retrieve: One-shot per task: skills are retrieved once when a new task is faced (before code generation), then injected into the GPT-4 prompt for that task's iterative code-generation rounds.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule tied to the task lifecycle: retrieval is triggered whenever the automatic curriculum proposes a new task (at the start of solving that task). It is not confidence-, attention-, or learned-classifier-triggered.
reranking: None. A single similarity_search_with_score returns top-5; no second-stage reranker (no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking).
retrieved_context_refinement: None / minimal: retrieved skills are used as-is (their full code is inserted into the prompt). No decomposition, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of retrieved skills.
tool_document_engineering: Skill descriptions are LLM-engineered before indexing: a dedicated GPT-3.5 'skill' prompt summarizes each generated program into a concise NL description (synthetic-summary augmentation), and the embedding of that description (not the raw code) is the index key. The description is generated as a JS comment header for the function.
index_content_separation: Yes (lightweight): the retrievable index stores only the description embedding (key) while the heavy content (full program code) is the value loaded on retrieval; description is separated from code, a form of progressive disclosure (embed description, load code on demand).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Live-synchronized growing index with CRUD-like behavior: skills are added (and overwritten/rewritten if the same program_name recurs, with the old vectordb id deleted) during learning; the Chroma vectordb is kept synced with skills.json. Integration protocol is function-calling style execution via the Mineflayer JS API (not RapidAPI/REST/MCP).
tool_dependency_awareness: No explicit inter-skill dependency modeling in retrieval. Compositionality is achieved at code-generation time (new skills call previously written skills/control primitives), but retrieval itself does not model a dependency graph or prerequisites; all current skill code plus control primitives are made available as reusable building blocks.
how_retrieved_used: Skill reuse via prompt augmentation: the top-5 retrieved skill programs (plus fixed control-primitive APIs) are inserted into GPT-4's code-generation prompt as in-context exemplars / reusable building blocks, so GPT-4 can call or compose them when synthesizing the new skill. No fine-tuning; retrieval feeds in-context learning only.
planning_integration: Retrieve-then-generate at task time: the automatic curriculum proposes a task, GPT-3.5 generates a plan, relevant skills are retrieved, and GPT-4 then synthesizes/refines code via the iterative prompting loop. Retrieval is one-shot per task (plan-then-retrieve-then-code), not interleaved inside a tree search or per action step.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-task (per-answer/per-skill): one retrieval call per curriculum task before the code-generation rollout. The iterative self-improvement loop (up to 4 rounds) reuses the same retrieved skills; retrieval is not re-issued per CoT step or per code-execution round.
adaptation_mechanism: Execution-feedback-driven adaptation under in-context reuse: retrieved skills serve as ICL exemplars/callable building blocks, and the freshly generated program is iteratively revised using environment feedback, execution errors, and a self-verification critique (not verbatim replay, not RL fine-tuning). (Voyager is not framed as CBR.)
retrieved_item_representation: Executable program/skill: the surface form injected into the prompt is raw JavaScript skill code (async functions) plus a descriptive comment header, not a distilled strategy, free-text workflow, or latent token.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Procedural skill: a reusable, temporally-extended, compositional executable program (higher abstraction than a raw trajectory or single demonstration; lower than a free-text strategy).
noise_robustness_mechanism: No dedicated retrieval-noise mechanism. Robustness comes from the downstream iterative prompting loop: self-verification (GPT-4 critic), environment feedback, and execution errors let GPT-4 ignore/repair unsuitable retrieved skills; there is no retriever-aware training or relevance evaluator gating the retrieved skills.
memory_type: skill-library (procedural memory of executable code skills), implemented as a vector database; plus a lightweight event/log checkpoint. Primary retrievable memory is the skill library.
write_back: Yes. Each time GPT-4 generates and self-verifies a new skill, the skill (code + GPT-3.5 description + description embedding) is written into the skill library / Chroma vectordb.
online_growth: Yes. The skill library is 'ever-growing': it starts empty and expands continuously during deployment/lifelong learning; it is not frozen after an offline phase.
write_back_trigger: On-success only (after self-verification): a skill is added to the library only once the GPT-4 self-verification critic validates the task as completed. Failed attempts are not stored as skills (the deposit/chest housekeeping skill is also explicitly excluded). If the same program_name recurs, the new version overwrites the old vectordb entry.
failure_experience_usage: Success-only for the persistent skill library: only verified/successful skills are retained and retrieved. Failure information (execution errors, critic critiques, environment feedback) is used transiently within the same task's iterative prompting rounds for self-improvement, but is not stored or retrieved as failure memory.
memory_evolution_update: Mostly append-only with refine-overwrite on name collision: new verified skills are appended; if a skill with the same program_name is regenerated, the old entry is deleted from the vectordb and rewritten (versioned on disk as nameV2/V3...). No dedup-merge across different names, no forgetting/pruning, no delta linking.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No. Retrieval is fixed top-k cosine similarity over frozen embeddings; case/skill selection is not a learned or RL-optimized policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Single-agent private memory by design, but the learned skill library is explicitly shown to be plug-and-play across frameworks: loading Voyager's skill library into AutoGPT improves AutoGPT's zero-shot task success, demonstrating transferable/shareable skills. No multi-agent shared memory during learning.
benchmarks: MineDojo-based custom Minecraft evaluation: (1) exploration performance (unique items discovered within 160 prompting iterations), (2) Minecraft tech-tree mastery (wooden -> stone -> iron -> diamond tools), (3) map coverage / distance traversed, (4) zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks in a new world (Diamond Pickaxe, Golden Sword, Lava Bucket, Compass). Built on MineDojo + Mineflayer.
benchmark_family: embodied (Minecraft). Custom Minecraft tasks built on MineDojo/Mineflayer rather than a standard fixed benchmark suite.
baselines: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), and AutoGPT (re-implemented with GPT-4 for task decomposition). All re-interpreted to run in MineDojo with environment feedback / agent state. Also internal variants: Voyager w/o Skill Library, and AutoGPT augmented with Voyager's skill library.
key_metrics: Number of unique items discovered (exploration); prompting iterations to unlock each tech-tree level (efficiency, lower is better) with success fraction out of 3 trials; distance traversed (map coverage); zero-shot task success fraction and prompting iterations to solve unseen tasks.
headline_result: Voyager obtains 3.3x more unique items, travels 2.3x longer distances, and unlocks the wooden-tool tech-tree milestone up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA; it discovers 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations and is the only method to unlock the diamond tool. In zero-shot transfer to a new world it solves all 4 unseen tasks while ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT solve none.
ablations: Six design choices ablated on exploration: automatic curriculum (random curriculum drops discovered-item count by 93%; manual curriculum underperforms), skill library (removing it causes performance to plateau in later stages and the agent only reaches up to iron, never diamond), environment feedback, execution errors, self-verification (most important feedback type; removal -73% discovered items), and GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 for code generation (GPT-4 yields 5.7x more unique items). Skill library is specifically shown to drive compounding/late-stage gains and zero-shot generalization; it is also transferable (boosts AutoGPT).
evaluation_decoupling: No. Only end-to-end task/exploration metrics are reported; no intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k, nDCG, retrieval completeness) are measured for the skill-retrieval step.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Primarily outcome-oriented but with strong process/efficiency signals: besides final success it reports prompting-iteration efficiency to reach milestones, exploration trajectory (item discovery over iterations), and map traversal, which capture intermediate progress rather than only final success.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Discussed qualitatively as a limitation: GPT-4 API is ~15x more expensive than GPT-3.5 but necessary for the code-generation quality (GPT-3.5 gives 5.7x fewer items). Efficiency is reported as prompting iterations to reach milestones (e.g., diamond reached at ~102 iterations in 1/3 trials; wooden at ~6 iterations). No explicit dollar cost or latency table; embedding/retrieval cost is negligible relative to GPT-4 calls.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed-k selection: top-5 retrieved skills (retrieval_top_k=5), capped at the current library size. No explicit token-budget cap or adaptive/precision-driven k; retrieved skill code plus control-primitive APIs and state are concatenated into the GPT-4 prompt.
survey_scope_and_axes: N/A (this is a method paper, not a survey).
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (no released standalone benchmark dataset; evaluation is a custom MineDojo/Mineflayer Minecraft protocol over exploration, tech-tree, map coverage, and 4 zero-shot tasks, each averaged over 3 trials with 160 (learning) / 50 (zero-shot) max prompting iterations).
cbr_cycle_coverage: [uncertain] Not framed as CBR; loosely maps to Retrieve (top-5 skills) + Reuse (in-context skill calls) + Revise (iterative self-improvement of generated code) + Retain (write verified skill to library), i.e. [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain], but Revise/Retain operate on the newly generated program rather than on the retrieved case.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it describes a skill library / retrieval-augmented code generation. CBR mechanisms are realized only implicitly.
builds_on: GPT-4 (OpenAI) for blackbox code generation; MineDojo (Fan et al. 2022) and Mineflayer for the Minecraft environment and high-level control API; ReAct and Reflexion for prompting/self-reflection ideas; AutoGPT for task decomposition; DreamCoder (Ellis et al. 2020) for the program-as-skill / library-growth inspiration; chain-of-thought prompting; OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 + Chroma vector store for skill retrieval.
contrasts_with: ReAct, Reflexion, and AutoGPT (which lack a growing skill library, self-verification, and automatic curriculum); pixel-to-low-level-control Minecraft agents such as VPT, MineDojo-based RL, DEPS, and other gradient/RL approaches (positioned as orthogonal, since Voyager uses a high-level code API rather than learning sensorimotor control); self-reflection-only methods (Voyager's self-verification both checks success and reflects).
lineage: Group F (decision-making / memory / RL agents): an early and highly influential example of a retrieval-augmented, self-growing procedural skill-library agent. Pioneers code-as-skill lifelong memory retrieved by embedding similarity, a lineage continued by works such as JARVIS-1, GITM, and later skill/workflow-memory agents (e.g., AWM, Agent Workflow Memory); contrasts with static-corpus RAG planners.
